column1: # retire-list.tsv — THE RETIRE LIST. It names every estate file a release has SUPERSEDED, and it
# is the ONLY thing `install.sh --upgrade` will ever retire.
# WHY IT IS DATA AND NOT INFERENCE. Nothing on a file system says that one file supersedes
# another. An upgrade that worked it out from what it found would eventually work it out wrong on
# somebody's estate, and the file it moved would be one they wanted. So supersession is DECLARED
# here, by the release that performed it, and the installer reads rather than reasons.
# WHY IT IS CUMULATIVE. A row is added when a release supersedes a path and is NEVER pruned.
# Most upgrades will SKIP RELEASES — an installed estate has no remote, so nobody is watching for
# releases — and a list describing only the newest release's supersessions would leave every file
# retired by an intermediate release sitting in the estate forever, for exactly the people who
# upgrade least often. Because the list is cumulative and the installer retires every listed path
# it actually FINDS, an upgrade across any span of releases retires everything across that span,
# with nothing to compare and no arithmetic to get wrong.
# WHAT RETIREMENT IS. The installer MOVES the file into a quarantine folder inside the estate and
# reports the move at the moment it happens, naming the command that puts it back. It is never a
# delete — never, under any circumstance — and it is never applied to a record: a row naming
# a path outside the machinery trees is REFUSED out loud and the file is left where it is.
# FORMAT — one row per superseded path, TAB-delimited, TWO fields:
#   <estate-relative path><TAB><what replaced it, in one sentence>
# Lines starting with "#" and blank lines are ignored. The path is spelled as it appears
# in an INSTALLED estate (no `estate/` prefix): `_harness/scripts/foo.sh`, not `estate/...`.
# THERE IS NO VERSION FIELD, AND ITS ABSENCE IS THE POINT (#298). It used to be column one. It was
# only ever REPORTED to the user — nothing filtered, compared or branched on it, because the list
# is cumulative precisely so that no version arithmetic is ever needed. Six rows here carried a
# stamp that was never true (they named a release that was still shipping the very files they
# claimed it had superseded), no check could have caught it, and a field that is unused and
# uncheckable is a claim the estate cannot keep. A tag on the project's code host is now the only
# version artifact this project has.
# EXAMPLE ROW, shown commented out so it is never acted on:
#   _harness/scripts/old-name.sh
# THE THREE ROWS BELOW ARE THIS LIST'S FIRST (#280). They are not renames — they are removals,
# which is the other way a path becomes superseded: the product no longer ships these three, so an
# estate installed before this release is holding machinery that nothing calls. Retirement is what
# takes them out of that estate without deleting anything: each is MOVED into `_retired/` and the
# command that puts it back is printed as it moves.
# WHY THESE THREE WENT. None had a job in the workflow this harness is for, and nothing called any
# of them. A session record restates where a ticket now stands, which is judgement, not stamping —
# a person writes it, or `ticket-scribe` does. A check is recorded as a REAL executable notebook
# cell through `append_notebook_cell.py` and run by the operator, which binds the output to the
# cell that produced it; transcribing a shell command's output into markdown is the weaker record.
# And a pure transport helper that executes nothing is a copy-and-paste an editor already does.
_harness/scripts/append_entry.sh

column1: # THE THREE ROWS AFTER THOSE (#140) ARE THE LIST'S FIRST TRUE RENAMES — the same path under a new
# name, which is what the format was written for. Each estate document was named after where it
# sits in the project rather than what a reader gets from opening it, and all three are
# root-pinned, so upgrade_is_machinery reads them as machinery and will retire them.
# WHY A RENAME STILL NEEDS A ROW. The replacement is laid down by the ordinary create arm the
# moment the new name is absent, so WITHOUT these rows an upgraded estate would simply hold both
# names — the old constitution beside the new one, each claiming to be the law. The row is what
# moves the old one out, and the printed restore command is what makes that survivable for a user
# who had edited their copy: their text is in quarantine, named, with the mv that puts it back.

column1: # THE SIX ROWS BELOW (#141) SETTLE EVERY SHIPPED SCRIPT ON ONE NAMING CONVENTION. The estate ran
# two spellings at once — six scripts separated words with an underscore, four with a hyphen — and
# nothing decided which was the house style. The hyphen won because it already was: the rest of
# the tree is lowercase-kebab, and the one name a user types most (harness-status.sh) was already
# spelled that way, so settling the other direction would have churned the most visible name in
# the product to gain nothing.
# THESE ARE RENAMES, NOT REMOVALS. Every one of the six still ships and still does the same job —
# only the spelling of its filename moved. An estate that skips this release and upgrades later
# gets the same treatment, because the list is cumulative and the installer retires every listed
# path it actually finds.
# THE HOOK CONFIGURATION IS THE ONE TO WATCH. .github/hooks/harness.json is written at install
# time and carries the validator path; it is a file the USER owns, so an upgrade carries it
# forward byte-identical rather than rewriting it. An estate upgrading across this release keeps
# a hook config naming check_ticket_log.sh, which the retirement has just moved to quarantine.
# Re-copy _harness/hooks/hooks.example.json over it to pick the new name up.
_harness/scripts/append_notebook_cell.py

column1: # THE ROW BELOW (#298) RETIRES THE VERSION STAMP ITSELF, which is why this list's own format
# changed in the same release. `VERSION` was a shipped, root-pinned file holding a release number,
# read by the installer and by harness-status and echoed by both. Nothing ever computed with it:
# no comparison, no arithmetic, no branch anywhere. It was a label, and labels drift.
# WHAT ANSWERS "AM I CURRENT?" NOW is both older and better: `install.sh --upgrade --dry-run`
# against a source checkout either says NOTHING TO DO or lists exactly what differs, file by file.
# That compares FILES. A stamp compared labels.
# WHY THE FILE DOES NOT SIMPLY VANISH. Estates installed before this release are holding a VERSION
# file that nothing reads any more; without this row it would sit at the estate root forever, a
# stale number no tool would ever correct and no user would think to doubt. Retirement moves it
# into `_retired/` and prints the command that puts it back.
VERSION
column2: removed — nothing in the machinery states a version any more; a tag on the project's code host is the only version artifact (#298)
